title: Quentin and the Orchard
premise: In 1911, in the river town of Vellmarsh, apprentice clockmaker Kestrel Thackeray is sent to repair the observatory's failing master clock and discovers, hidden in its case, a sealed letter naming the Thackeray family among conspirators in a treasonous smuggling ring. The letter's author is Odile Marchand, daughter of a neighboring orchard-owning family now declared enemy aliens after a diplomatic rupture, to whom Kestrel made a quiet promise in peacetime: that he would keep her family's name safe. As investigators close in and his own master betrays him to save the guild, Kestrel must choose between duty to his craft, his country, and the girl he loves — ultimately dismantling the clock to destroy the letter's evidence, testifying that the mechanism itself was faulty, and fleeing with Odile as the orchard burns behind them.
about_author: Ivo Oyelaran is the pen name of a former watch restorer who spent a decade repairing antique mechanisms in museum archives before turning to fiction. His novels are known for their precision-engineered plots and their tender attention to objects that outlive the people who make them.

chapters.title: The Weight of Small Gears
chapters.summary: Kestrel Thackeray, POV. Summoned to the Vellmarsh observatory to repair the master clock that keeps the whole town's time, Kestrel measures his modest life against the guild's grandeur. He recalls his childhood promise to Odile Marchand of the orchard estate. The beat is longing tempered by duty — a man who trusts mechanisms more than people.

chapters.title: A Letter in the Works
chapters.summary: Kestrel, POV. Opening the clock's case to replace a broken escapement, he finds a sealed letter naming the Thackerays in a smuggling conspiracy — signed by Odile's father. He hides it, shaken, unsure whether it's evidence or a trap. The beat is dread: the ordered world of gears has revealed a hidden, dangerous mechanism.

chapters.title: The Orchard in Winter
chapters.summary: Odile Marchand, POV. With her family declared enemy aliens and the estate under watch, Odile walks the bare orchard and writes to the one person she still trusts — not knowing her father's letter already sits in Kestrel's pocket. The beat is isolation and stubborn hope, love persisting against official hatred.

chapters.title: What the Guild Requires
chapters.summary: Kestrel, POV. His master, Ambrose Pell, notices Kestrel's distraction and quietly reports the observatory visit to the investigators, trading Kestrel's silence for the guild's protection. Kestrel realizes he is being watched. The beat is betrayal — the mentor who taught him precision uses it to corner him.

chapters.title: Midnight at the Observatory
chapters.summary: Kestrel, POV, with a brief Odile interlude. Risking arrest, Kestrel meets Odile at night beneath the observatory; they compare what they know and realize the conspiracy implicates half the town's respectable families. The beat is rekindled love fused with shared danger — a promise made in peacetime now costing everything.

chapters.title: The Investigator's Patience
chapters.summary: Investigator Harrow, POV. Harrow, methodical and weary, closes the net on the Marchand estate and begins pulling at the Thackeray name. He offers Kestrel immunity to inform. The beat is tightening pressure; the antagonist is not cruel but inexorable, like time itself.

chapters.title: Escapement
chapters.summary: Kestrel, POV. Cornered by Pell and Harrow both, Kestrel flees to the orchard, where soldiers have begun inventorying the Marchand property. Odile's father, dying, asks Kestrel to protect his daughter and the letter both — two promises that now contradict each other. The beat is moral crisis.

chapters.title: The Master Clock Stops
chapters.summary: Kestrel, POV. In the climax, Kestrel dismantles the observatory's master clock before the town, publicly declaring the mechanism faulty and feeding the letter into the works, destroying the evidence and the town's shared time with it. Harrow arrests him amid chaos. The beat is sacrifice — he breaks his craft to keep his word.

chapters.title: Testimony
chapters.summary: Kestrel, POV. At his hearing, Kestrel refuses to name the Marchands or the conspirators, arguing that a broken clock cannot testify and neither should a broken man. Odile appears unexpectedly, claiming the letter as her own correspondence. The beat is quiet defiance; love and identity outweigh duty's demands.

chapters.title: What Can Be Carried
chapters.summary: Kestrel and Odile, alternating POV. Released with the case collapsed, they leave Vellmarsh at dawn with only what they can carry — a few tools, a sapling from the orchard — as smoke rises behind them. In a new town, Kestrel builds a small clock that runs a little slow, on purpose. The beat is bittersweet resolution: inheritance is not what we're given but what we choose to keep.
